A0030.title: Business-Level Honeypot
A0030.definition: A fake business resource system built specifically for attackers rather than normal users.
A0030.description: This resource system must ensure that it is not accessed by normal users during regular business access or request processes, but can be discovered and exploited by attackers through methods such as resource ID enumeration, reverse engineering, packet capture, or cracking. In this way, any access to the fake business resource system identifies the visitor as an attacker, enabling immediate alerts that business resources have been targeted and attacked, and allowing continuous tracking of the attacker's identity, characteristics, and behavior to facilitate evasion technique upgrades or related countermeasures.
A0030.limitation: Ineffective against attacks that fully mimic normal user access behavior; advanced attackers can identify and evade honeypot resources or remove honeypot tracking points by comparing them with normal business processes. Improper trap design may inadvertently affect normal users or be indexed by search engines, requiring continuous updates to trap forms to maintain an adversarial advantage.

references.title: Guide to Intrusion Detection and Prevention Systems (IDPS)

A0030-001.title: Dynamic Beaconing and Honeypot Traps
A0030-001.definition: Active perception sub-measures — dynamic beacons, loop traps, fake timestamps, hidden honeypot resource IDs/APIs, special-function popups, and dynamic HTTP header injection — that induce attackers to expose themselves and enable continuous tracking of their behavioral characteristics.
A0030-001.description: Dynamic instrumentation and honeypot traps are active sensing sub-mechanisms of business-level honeypots (A0030). Specific forms include: dynamic instrumentation (dynamically inserting hidden tracking points in pages that normal users would not trigger but crawlers would request, where triggering immediately marks the access as automated), loop traps (constructing fake resources that trap crawlers in infinite loops or repeated requests, consuming their resources and exposing their behavior), fake timestamps/fake parameters (mixing deceptive timestamps or parameters into responses to induce crawlers to collect incorrect data), hidden honeypot resource IDs and honeypot API endpoints (fake resources not exposed in normal business flows and only discoverable through resource enumeration or reverse engineering), special feature pop-ups (advertisements, red envelopes, and other features visible to normal users but abnormally interacted with by crawlers, used to collect crawler interaction characteristics), and dynamic HTTP header injection (dynamically adding honeypot marker headers in responses to track whether crawlers carry them back in subsequent requests). The common goal of these mechanisms is to make automated visitors actively expose themselves without affecting normal users, enabling the server to continuously track the attacker's identity, characteristics, and behavioral patterns, thereby providing a basis for upgrading evasion countermeasures and taking enforcement actions.
A0030-001.limitation: The effectiveness of dynamic instrumentation and honeypot traps depends on stealth; once the honeypot resources or instrumentation logic are identified and evaded by attackers, they become ineffective. Advanced attackers can filter out honeypot requests through behavioral analysis and comparison with normal business flows. Improper trap design may inadvertently harm legitimate users or cause negative impacts if indexed by search engines. Trap forms must be continuously updated to maintain a competitive advantage.
